topic: R155 post-production phase definition (how long CSMS obligations run)
figure: Post-production phase = from end of production of the vehicle type until end-of-life of all vehicles of that type (no fixed number of years)
quote: "Post-production phase" refers to the period in which a vehicle type is no longer produced until the end-of-life of all vehicles under the vehicle type.
source: EUR-Lex — UN Regulation No 155 (EU publication, OJ L 2025/5, 42025X0005), definition 2.7
geography: UNECE 1958 Agreement contracting parties incl. EU, UK, Japan, Korea
note: Regulation text, read from the search result only (unece.org and eur-lex.europa.eu would not resolve for WebFetch). Same result says the phase ends when no operational vehicles of the type remain.

topic: R155 CSMS phases covered
figure: CSMS must cover development, production AND post-production phases
quote: the vehicle manufacturer shall demonstrate to an Approval Authority or Technical Service that their Cyber Security Management System applies to the following phases [development, production, post-production]
source: UN R155 para 7.2.2.1, as quoted by SIP-adus workshop slides (Kawana) and secrss.com translation of the R155 interpretation document
note: Regulation paragraph quoted through a secondary deck; bracketed phase list is the search summary's, not verbatim.

topic: R155 monitoring / response obligation over vehicle life
figure: Processes to monitor for, detect and respond to cyber-attacks/threats/vulnerabilities on vehicle types; monitoring continual and includes vehicles after first registration
quote: UN R155 paragraph 7.2.2.2(g) requires manufacturers to have processes for monitoring, detecting and responding to cyber threats on vehicle types ... Paragraph 7.2.2.4 requires that monitoring be continual. It must include vehicles after first registration
source: EUR-Lex — UN Regulation No 155 (OJ L 2025/5) paras 7.2.2.2(g), 7.2.2.4; UNECE interpretation document WP29-182-05
note: PARAPHRASE by the search tool of the regulation text, not the verbatim wording. Interpretation document (https://unece.org/fileadmin/DAM/trans/doc/2020/wp29/WP29-182-05e.pdf) says the aim is to cover already type-approved vehicles so the manufacturer can respond in a timely way. Verbatim text of 7.2.2.2(h) ('reasonable timeframe') NOT confirmed.

topic: R155 reporting frequency to approval authority
figure: At least once a year (or on request)
quote: The manufacturer shall report at least once per year, or upon request, to the approval authority on the outcome of the monitoring activities, including information on new attacks.
source: The Art of Service compliance control library — UNECE WP.29 R155 CSMS monitor (paraphrase of R155 para 7.4.1)
note: Secondary paraphrase; a second search result attributed 'at least once a year' to the EUR-Lex R155 text but the verbatim 7.4.1 wording was not retrieved.

topic: R155 CSMS certificate validity
figure: CSMS Certificate of Compliance valid max 3 years (renewal recurs while the CSMS must be maintained)
quote: The SUMS certificate shall remain valid for a maximum of three years from the date of deliverance of the certificate unless it is withdrawn. However, existing vehicle type approvals shall not lose their validity due to the expiration of the manufacturer's Certificate of Compliance.
source: UN Regulation No 156 text (UNECE R156e PDF / EUR-Lex 42021X0388), paras 6.6 / 6.10
note: This quote is R156 (SUMS). R155 has an equivalent 3-year CSMS certificate clause — NOT confirmed in this search; do not assume.

topic: R156 software updates over vehicle lifetime
figure: Software updates must be possible at any point during the lifetime of the vehicles (no number of years stated)
quote: uniform provisions on ensuring software updates (with/without hardware changes/upgrades) can be performed at any point of time during the lifetime of the vehicles
source: UNECE — UN Regulation No. 156 presentation (François Guichard, GRE-85-36)
note: UNECE secretariat presentation, not the regulation text. Search found NO post-production retention period (no 'X years after end of production') in R156.

topic: R156 record-keeping per update
figure: Records for each update applied to a vehicle type; information available for type approval, CoP, market surveillance, recalls and PTI
quote: The vehicle manufacturer shall record, and store, the following information for each update applied to a given vehicle type ... information available ... for the purpose of type approval, conformity of production, market surveillance, recalls and Periodic Technical Inspection (PTI)
source: UN Regulation No 156 (UNECE R156e PDF; EUR-Lex 42021X0388), paras 7.1.2, 7.1.1.12
note: Two clauses joined by the search summary ('...'). An RDW workshop paper (https://unece.org/sites/default/files/2022-11/SoftwareUpdate_Post_Registration.pdf) states R155/R156 'does not address post-registration updates precisely'.

topic: R156 approval continuity after production ends (proposed amendment)
figure: Production not considered definitively discontinued while manufacturer intends approval extensions for updates to registered vehicles
quote: the production is not considered definitively discontinued if the vehicle manufacturer intends to obtain subsequent extensions of the approval for software updates of vehicles already registered in the market
source: UNECE IWG on CS/OTA informal document (GRVA-21-06 or GRVA-16-15)
note: PROPOSED amendment in a working-group paper; not adopted text as far as this search shows. Exact document of the two (GRVA-21-06 / GRVA-16-15) not certain from the snippet.

topic: EU Cyber Resilience Act scope — vehicles
figure: Vehicles type-approved under Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 are excluded from the CRA (Art 2(2)(c))
quote: Motor vehicles are excluded by Article 2(2)(c). Recital 27 points to the type-approval regime under Regulation 2019/2144, which incorporates the UNECE rules on vehicle cybersecurity and software updates.
source: Automotive IQ — 'Article 2(2)(c) Exempts Your Vehicle From the EU Cyber Resilience Act. It Doesn't Exempt What You Bolted to It'; springlex.eu CRA Article 2 (OJ L 2024/2847)
note: Same result: aftermarket connected devices, EV chargers and standalone diagnostic tools sold outside 2019/2144 remain in CRA scope. CRA Article text page: https://www.springlex.eu/en/packages/cra/cra-regulation/article-2/

topic: EU Cyber Resilience Act support period (ADJACENT — does NOT apply to type-approved vehicles)
figure: Support period at least 5 years, unless the product's expected use time is shorter
quote: the support period shall be at least five years ... the support period shall correspond to the expected use time
source: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 Article 13(8), as reproduced by springlex.eu / eucybersecurity.org
note: NOT a vehicle obligation (vehicles excluded by Art 2(2)(c)). Recorded only as the nearest statutory support-period benchmark, and for aftermarket/charger products that stay in scope.

topic: ISO/SAE 21434 — end of cybersecurity support
figure: Vulnerability management continues until 'end of cybersecurity support' (date set by the organisation, no fixed years); Clause 14 covers end of support and decommissioning
quote: Clause 8 Continual cybersecurity activities includes activities that provide information for ongoing risk assessments and defines vulnerability management of E/E systems until end of cybersecurity support. ... Clause 14 End of cybersecurity support and decommissioning includes cybersecurity considerations for end of support and decommissioning of an item or component.
source: Secondary summaries of ISO/SAE 21434:2021 (TÜV NORD whitepaper; COVESA/GENIVI ISO 21434 summary; UL training pages)
note: Normative text is paywalled — not read. Exact RQ-14-xx wording NOT confirmed. A Chinese translation (https://www.cnblogs.com/walker-lee/p/18840782.html, Low) lists RQ-05-12 (configuration info kept until end of cybersecurity support) and RC-05-15 (reproducible environment for incident remediation kept until then).

topic: ISO/SAE 21434 — communication of end of support
figure: Organisation defines and communicates end-of-support and decommissioning conditions
quote: The organisation defines and communicates end of cybersecurity support and decommissioning conditions for items including data destruction.
source: The Art of Service — ISO/SAE 21434 control 21434-14
note: Paraphrase by a control library, not the standard's wording.

topic: China GB 44495-2024 lifecycle CSMS
figure: CSMS across vehicle lifecycle; mandatory from 2026-01-01 (new types); applies to M, N and O (with ≥1 ECU)
quote: manufacturers need to establish and maintain a vehicle cybersecurity management system throughout the vehicle lifecycle and development phase [TÜV SÜD interpretation]; 将于 2026 年 1 月 1 日起开始实施
source: TÜV SÜD — 'China implements vehicle cybersecurity technical requirements'; ithome.com
note: The standard's own post-production-phase definition and any vulnerability response deadline were NOT FOUND (full text paid: https://www.chinesestandard.net/PDF.aspx/GB44495-2024). Quote is the search summary's rendering of TÜV SÜD, not verbatim.

topic: In-house SOC operating cost (ADJACENT — enterprise IT SOC, NOT a vehicle SOC)
figure: USD 2.86 million per year (Ponemon); USD 2–7 million per year (Arctic Wolf); 24/7 seat = 4.2–5 FTE
quote: Ponemon at about $2.86 million per year for an in-house SOC ... anywhere from $2 million to $7 million annually ... A single 24/7 seat needs 4.2 to 5 full time analysts once you account for shifts, PTO, and burnout.
source: Arctic Wolf — 'How Much Does It Cost to Build a SOC'; UnderDefense SOC cost calculator
note: Vendor marketing about enterprise SOCs; NOT automotive VSOC. Recorded only as an adjacent figure.

topic: OTA data cost (fleet)
figure: > USD 1 billion per year and > 20 PB for a 10-million-vehicle fleet; IVI update ≈ 500 MB per vehicle per update
quote: According to a new Guidehouse Insights report, the cost of data transmission for a 10-million vehicle fleet can reach over 20 PB of data and cost over $1 Billion, every year! ... for an in-vehicle infotainment system (IVI) update, the file size can be 500MB per vehicle, per update, on average.
source: IIoT World blog citing Guidehouse Insights
note: Secondary blog; the Guidehouse report itself not read. Covers ALL connected-vehicle data transmission, not OTA alone (as worded). See derivation in cyber-tail.md.
derivation: USD 1,000,000,000 / 10,000,000 vehicles = USD 100 per vehicle per year (lower bound from 'over $1 Billion'); NOT a published figure.
